metadata.title: How to Patch a Capacitor Plugin (Bun, npm, pnpm)
metadata.description: How to patch a Capacitor plugin with bun patch, patch-package or pnpm patch, apply native iOS and Android fixes, and decide when to fork or upstream.
metadata.author: Martin Donadieu

faq.question: Can I patch the native iOS and Android code of a Capacitor plugin?
faq.answer: Yes. Capacitor builds plugin native code straight from node_modules (Gradle includes the plugin's android folder, CocoaPods and SPM point to the plugin path). Patch the Swift, Kotlin, Java, Gradle, podspec or Package.swift files, then run cap sync and rebuild the app.

faq.question: Do I need patch-package if I use Bun?
faq.answer: No. Bun has built-in patching: bun patch <pkg>, edit the files, then bun patch --commit. Bun stores the diff in patches/ and records it under patchedDependencies in package.json, and reapplies it on every bun install.

faq.question: Can I ship a plugin patch with a live update?
faq.answer: Only if the change is in the plugin's JavaScript, which ends up in your web bundle. Native changes in Swift, Kotlin, Gradle or podspec files require a new App Store and Google Play build.

faq.question: What happens to my patch when I upgrade the plugin?
faq.answer: Patches are tied to an exact version. With Bun the key includes the version, so an upgrade needs a fresh patch. patch-package tries to apply the old diff and fails loudly if it no longer fits. Check whether the upstream release already contains the fix first.

faq.question: When should I fork instead of patching?
faq.answer: Fork when the change is large, touches many files, adds features, or must live for months. A long patch is hard to review and breaks on every upgrade. A fork published under your own npm scope is easier to version and test.

Patching is the right move when a plugin has a small bug, a version constraint that blocks your build, or an upstream fix that's merged but not released. This guide covers the workflow for each package manager, how native patches reach Xcode and Gradle, and when a fork or an upstream PR is the better call.

Example: fix a native build error in a plugin
A common case: your app uses AGP 9, and an older plugin's
, which AGP 9 rejects. You can't wait for a release.

bun patch --commit node_modules/some-capacitor-plugin
bunx cap sync android
cd android && ./gradlew assembleDebug

Fork, or switch to a maintained plugin
If you fork, publish it so installs stay reproducible:

# in the fork, rename to your scope in package.json: "@acme/capacitor-foo"
bun run build
bun publish --access restricted
Installing from a git URL also works, but the plugin's
folder must exist in that branch or be built by a
script, and not every package manager runs dependency lifecycle scripts by default. A published package avoids that.
